opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's actually a funny origin point, because people usually expect a math person to come to AI through something very technical. But I got interested through law first.

When I was at Oxford and then later thinking about legal reasoning, I was fascinated by how constitutional interpretation works. You have a fixed, very short text, and then centuries of people arguing about what it means: originalism, textualism, living constitutionalism. And the question I kept coming back to was, can a machine actually *reason* about this, or is it just pattern-matching on how judges have written in the past?

What I realized pretty quickly is that law is a really hard domain to evaluate. If a model gives you an interpretation of the Fourth Amendment, who's to say it's right? You can have two brilliant justices disagree, nine to zero becomes five to four depending on the decade. There's no ground truth. So you can't really build a feedback loop where the system gets better by checking itself against reality.

And that's what pushed me toward mathematics. Math has the same flavor I loved about law: you start from a small set of foundational statements, axioms instead of constitutional clauses, and you build these long chains of argument from them. But the crucial difference is that in math, especially with formal languages like Lean, you can *verify*. A proof either checks or it doesn't. There's no five-to-four.

So in a way, the law project taught me what was missing. Reasoning without verification is very hard to scale, because the model can sound extremely convincing while being wrong, and you can't tell. With formal math, you get a perfect verifier for free, and that changes everything. It means you can do search, you can do reinforcement learning, you can generate enormous amounts of reasoning and keep only what's provably correct.

I still think about legal reasoning, honestly. I think a lot of what we learn building mathematical reasoners, how to structure arguments, how to decompose a big claim into lemmas, will eventually flow back into domains like law. But math felt like the right place to start, because it's the one place where you can actually know when the AI is right.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good place to start, because the Constitution project really was the seed for everything that came after.

When I was at MIT, I got interested in a very simple question: if you took a large language model and gave it the text of the Constitution plus hundreds of years of Supreme Court opinions, could it actually reason the way a constitutional lawyer does? Not just retrieve the right precedent, but construct an argument, anticipate the counterargument, and arrive at a defensible interpretation. And what I found was that the models were surprisingly good at the surface of legal reasoning and surprisingly bad at the structure of it. They could sound like Justice Scalia. They could not reliably tell you whether the argument they'd just made was internally consistent.

That gap stuck with me. Law is interesting because it looks like it has rules, but underneath it is fundamentally about persuasion. Two brilliant people can read the same clause and reach opposite conclusions, and there is no oracle that tells you who is right. So when a model produces a confident interpretation, you have no ground truth to check it against. You can only ask whether it's convincing.

Mathematics is the exact opposite. In math, there is a ground truth. A proof is either valid or it isn't. And that realization was the turning point for me. I thought, if the hard problem with AI reasoning is that we can't verify it, then let's go work in the one domain where verification is not only possible but has been formalized for decades. Proof assistants like Lean give you a compiler for truth. The model can hallucinate as much as it wants, but if the proof doesn't type-check, it doesn't count.

So in a strange way, the Constitution project taught me what I didn't want. I didn't want to build systems whose output I had to take on faith, no matter how eloquent. I wanted to build systems where the output comes with a certificate. Math gives you that, and I came to believe it's the right training ground for reasoning more broadly. If you can teach a model to reason rigorously where cheating is impossible, you've learned something about how to make it reason honestly everywhere else.

And there's a second lesson that carried over. In law, the interesting part was never the easy cases. It was the hard cases, the ones at the frontier where existing precedent runs out and you have to extend the framework. Research mathematics is the same. The value isn't in redoing undergraduate exercises. It's in the open problems, where even the question of what to try is unclear. That's where I think AI can genuinely change the pace of discovery, and that's what we're trying to build toward at Axiom.

astra-6.text:
The connection, for me, is the question of what it means for an AI to reason within a set of rules. With the Constitution, you have a text, but applying it isn’t simply looking up a sentence. You have to interpret language, consider how different principles interact, and explain why a conclusion follows. That makes you ask whether an AI is actually reasoning or just producing a persuasive argument.

Mathematics gives you a particularly clear way to explore that distinction. You still need creativity to find a useful definition or an unexpected proof strategy, but once you have a proof, there’s a much more precise standard for checking it. A convincing explanation isn’t enough; the steps have to be valid.

So that idea points toward a combination I find exciting: AI that can explore possibilities creatively, paired with rigorous verification. Verification doesn’t tell you which questions are interesting or which approach will work, but it can help establish whether what you’ve found is correct.

sol-6.1.text:
The connection, for me, is about what it means to reason within a set of rules. With the Constitution, you have a text, but applying it to a new situation requires interpretation. Different people can start from the same words and reach different conclusions. That raises an interesting question for AI: is it following an argument, or reproducing patterns in arguments it has seen?

Mathematics gives you a setting where you can make that question more precise. Once you specify the definitions and assumptions, a proof has to justify each step. You can check whether the conclusion actually follows. But discovering that proof still requires creativity—choosing a useful representation, making a conjecture, or finding the right intermediate result. That combination of open-ended discovery and rigorous verification is what makes AI for mathematics so compelling to me.
